checks.claim: Symbiosis is a close, long-term interaction between two different species
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'any close and long-term interaction between two or more different biological species'; OpenStax: 'close interactions between individuals of different species over an extended period of time'.

checks.claim: Three kinds: mutualism, commensalism, parasitism
Key: the kind is decided by whether each partner is helped, harmed or neither
checks.note: Grokipedia sorts them 'by net effect': both benefit / one benefits, other unaffected / one benefits at the other's expense.

checks.claim: Wrong: which kind is larger; plants vs animals; how closely related
checks.note: None of these is a criterion in any source; all three are plainly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: in commensalism the other is neither helped nor harmed; in parasitism one gains at the other's cost; partners may be plant, animal or fungus
Key: bee and flower is mutualism
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'A prominent example of pollination mutualism is with bees and flowering plants.' Grokipedia Mutualism: 'bees transferring pollen between flowers while collecting nectar'.

checks.claim: Pollen sticks to the hairs on a bee's body and rubs off at the next flower
checks.note: Grokipedia: bees' electrostatic charge attracts pollen 'to their body hairs'.

checks.claim: Context: pollination lets the plant make seeds
checks.note: 'initiating fertilization and enabling seed and fruit development'.

checks.claim: Wrong: commensalism, parasitism, predation
checks.note: Both sides gain, so none of the three fits; the stem calls it an 'interaction', not symbiosis, which is correct since bee-flower is not a long-term living-together.

checks.claim: Trillions of bacteria live in the gut
checks.note: About 38 trillion bacterial cells (2016 estimate).

checks.claim: Key: they digest fibre the body cannot
checks.note: Microbes ferment fibre the body cannot digest into short-chain fatty acids the host absorbs.

checks.claim: Wrong: they make stomach acid
checks.note: Made by parietal cells of the stomach lining; bacteria have no role.

checks.claim: Wrong: they make the bile that digests fat
checks.note: Bile is made by liver hepatocytes, so the choice is wrong. Minor wording: bile emulsifies fat, it does not itself digest it (lipase does). Optional: 'They make the bile that helps break down fat'.

checks.claim: Wrong: they carry oxygen into the blood
checks.note: Red blood cells (haemoglobin) carry oxygen.

checks.claim: Context: most in the large intestine; make vitamins such as vitamin K; get a home and food; mutualism
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'synthesizing certain B vitamins and vitamin K'; mucus layer where microbes 'anchor and feed'; 'not merely commensal ... but rather a mutualistic relationship'; colon has the highest microbial density.

checks.claim: A lichen is a fungus and a green alga (or cyanobacterium) living together
checks.note: The stem's 'a green alga' is one of the two photobiont kinds; true for the lichen described.

checks.claim: Key: the alga gives the fungus food it makes from sunlight
checks.note: 'The fungi benefit from the carbohydrates produced by the algae or cyanobacteria via photosynthesis.'

checks.claim: Wrong: water soaked up from rain; minerals freed from rock; a shield against drying out
checks.note: Water retention, mineral capture and protection are the fungus's contributions ('The fungal partner protects the alga by retaining water'; 'a larger capture area for mineral nutrients'); no source credits the alga with giving water, minerals or a shield.

checks.claim: Context: alga's sugars feed both; fungus shelters and gathers water and minerals; mutualism; grows on bare rock
checks.note: Grokipedia: photobiont supplies carbohydrates 'which nourish both partners'; fungus gives 'structural support and protection' and 'access to water and minerals'; 'mutualistic'; 'pioneers on barren rocks'.

checks.claim: Peas, beans and clover grow root nodules packed with bacteria (rhizobia); both gain
checks.note: 'form mutualistic symbiotic associations with the roots of leguminous plants'; peas, clovers, common beans named.

checks.claim: Key: the bacteria give nitrogen taken from the air
checks.note: 'converting atmospheric dinitrogen (N2) into ammonia (NH3)' within root nodules.

checks.claim: Wrong: sugar made from sunlight; water from deep soil; oxygen from the soil
checks.note: The sugar flows the other way (plant to bacteria: 'in return for energy-containing carbohydrates'); nodules keep oxygen low (leghemoglobin); no water role.

checks.claim: Context: air is mostly nitrogen gas, which plants need but cannot use as it is
checks.note: N2 about 78% of the atmosphere; chemically inert (triple bond), unusable directly by most organisms, plants included.

checks.claim: Context: the plant pays them with sugar made in its leaves
checks.note: Bacteria get 'malate and sucrose derived from plant photosynthates'; 'sugar made in its leaves' is a fair grade-level simplification.

checks.claim: Context: farmers long grew such plants to keep their soil rich in nitrogen
checks.note: Legumes in rotation since Roman and medieval times (Norfolk four-course clover 'to fix nitrogen'); Boussingault (1830s) found legumes maintained or increased soil nitrogen (Grokipedia Nitrogen fixation). Early farmers did not know the reason was nitrogen; optional wording 'to keep their soil rich' avoids implying they did.

checks.claim: Orchid roots cling to bark, do not grow into the tree, soak up rain and mist
checks.note: Velamen 'absorbs and stores water' during rain or mist; epiphytes obtain water and nutrients 'without deriving nutrients or water from its host'.

checks.claim: Key: orchid on a tree is commensalism
checks.note: Grokipedia names orchids and bromeliads as inquilinism, a form of commensalism; Grokipedia Epiphyte: 'Epiphytism exemplifies a commensal interaction' ('in most cases'). Some researchers argue heavy epiphyte loads can harm branches by weight ('structural parasitism'), but evidence for orchids is thin and anecdotal; commensalism remains the standard answer, and the context already carries the caveat. Key is safe.

checks.claim: Wrong: parasitism
checks.note: Parasites 'penetrate host tissues via specialized haustoria'; the stem rules this out.

checks.claim: Wrong: mutualism, competition
checks.note: No source gives the tree a benefit or casts a single orchid as competing with its host.

checks.claim: Context: proving a host truly unaffected is hard; small costs or benefits can go unseen
checks.note: 'small, context-dependent costs or benefits may exist but remain undetected'.

checks.claim: Tick bites in, drinks blood for several days, drops off swollen
checks.note: Hard ticks feed for days (adult females 7-10 days), engorge, detach.

checks.claim: Key: parasitism
checks.note: Ticks are blood-feeding ectoparasites; white-tailed deer are key hosts of adult blacklegged ticks.

checks.claim: Wrong: predation
checks.note: A predator kills and eats its prey; the deer walks on. (Some ecological models frame ticks as 'micro-predators', per Grokipedia Tick, but at grade level and in the stem's situation, predation is not defensible.)

checks.claim: Wrong: commensalism, mutualism
checks.note: The deer is harmed (blood loss, anaemia, energy cost).

checks.claim: Context: 'the deer loses blood, and ticks can pass on diseases such as Lyme disease: one gains at the other's cost'
checks.note: Misleading in this scene: it reads as if the deer is harmed by catching Lyme disease. Deer do not get Lyme disease; Pennsylvania Game Commission: deer 'do not contract the disease when an infected tick feeds on them' and are 'a dead-end host'; Grokipedia Tick: reservoir competence 'negligible in deer'. Lyme is a harm to people, not to the deer. Fix: 'The tick gains a meal and the deer loses blood, and a heavy load of ticks can leave a deer weak: one gains at the other's cost, so it is parasitism.' (Grokipedia Tick: ticks impose 'energy depletion, anemia'.) If Lyme should stay, say it is passed to people: '...and the same ticks can pass Lyme disease to people.'

checks.claim: Context: a predator kills and eats its prey, while a parasite usually feeds on a host that lives on
checks.note: OpenStax: a parasite 'is unlikely to kill the host, especially not quickly'.

checks.claim: Mistletoe's green leaves make some of its own food; still called a parasite
checks.note: 'All mistletoe species are hemiparasites because they do perform some photosynthesis.'

checks.claim: Key: it grows into the branch to take water
checks.note: Haustorium 'penetrates the host's xylem to extract water and minerals', 'several centimeters into the host tissue'.

checks.claim: Wrong: coils round to choke; drips poison; soaks up rain on the tree
checks.note: Mistletoe grows as clumps from an attachment point; no coiling or poison. Soaking up rain is what epiphytes do and would not make it a parasite.

checks.claim: Context: root-like part draws water and minerals the tree carries up from its roots; a heavy load can stunt or kill a tree
checks.note: Hosts suffer 'reduced growth, stunting, and loss of infested outer branches'; 'A heavy infestation may also kill the host plant.'

checks.claim: Key: lynx peaks came a year or two after hare peaks
checks.note: 'Lynx densities typically peak 1 to 2 years after hare maxima'; OpenStax: predator 'lagging 1-2 years behind'. The stem's 'usually' covers stretches of the fur record where the pattern is messier.

checks.claim: Wrong: before the hares; same year; when hares were fewest
checks.note: Hare lows come several years after the hare peak, so a lynx peak 1-2 years after the hare peak falls during the hare decline, not at the hare low.

checks.claim: Both numbers rose and fell about every ten years
checks.note: 8-11 years (hares), 9-11 (lynx); OpenStax 'approximately 10 years'. Elton and Nicholson's cycles averaged about 9.6 years.

checks.claim: Stem: the Hudson's Bay Company kept records of the lynx AND snowshoe hare furs that trappers sold it, year after year, for close to a century
checks.note: The lynx half is solid (HBC lynx fur returns; Stenseth et al. 1997 PNAS give lynx series 1821-1939, longer than a century). The hare half is the textbook simplification: the classic 1845-1935 hare series (MacLulich) is two data sets, '1844-1904 represents fur records, whereas 1905-1935 derives from questionnaires' (Stenseth et al. 1997, PNAS), so the hare numbers were not furs sold for the whole century. Popular sources (tsibbledata 'trading records for Snowshoe Hare and Canadian Lynx furs from 1845 to 1935', Odum's graph) repeat the simple version. Safe fix: 'Canada's fur trade kept count of the lynx and snowshoe hares trappers took, year after year, for close to a century, most of it in the Hudson's Bay Company's records.' or 'The Hudson's Bay Company's fur records, with trappers' reports, tracked lynx and snowshoe hares for close to a century.'

checks.claim: Context: lynx live mostly on snowshoe hares; predator's peaks trail the prey's by one to two years; cycle about ten years
checks.note: Hares 40-96% of diet biomass, 60-90% in peak hare years.

checks.claim: Snowshoe hares are most of what lynx eat
checks.note: 'over 75% of its diet across its core boreal range'.

checks.claim: Stem: in some years the lynx catch so many that hares become rare
checks.note: OpenStax says the lynx 'kill so many hares that hare population begins to decline'. Field work (Krebs, Kluane) shows the decline is the work of several hunters (lynx, coyotes, great horned owls, goshawks), with predation the main driver. Grade-level simplification still true in part; optional wording 'lynx and other hunters catch so many'.

checks.claim: Key: as hares grow scarce, lynx grow fewer too (so the remaining hares recover)
checks.note: Starvation is a main cause of lynx death in hare lows; kitten survival near zero 1-2 years after a crash; fertility falls; many emigrate. OpenStax: 'When the lynx population is low, the hare population size begins to increase.' This is the honest core answer; the context also notes the role of hare food (Grokipedia Snowshoe hare: food added tripled densities; food plus predator removal gave over 10-fold).

checks.claim: Wrong: hares hide in burrows lynx cannot reach
checks.note: Hares rest in 'shallow depressions called forms'; they tunnel into snow only to reach forage.

checks.claim: Wrong: lynx stop hunting until hares recover
checks.note: Lynx keep hunting, starve or emigrate; they do not hold back.

checks.claim: Wrong: a sickness kills off lynx every ten years
checks.note: Lynx declines come from starvation, low kitten survival and emigration, not a ten-year disease.

checks.claim: Context: many lynx starve, few kittens survive; hares breed back up; food plays a part; hares rest in shallow hollows, not burrows
checks.note: Consistent with Grokipedia and OpenStax. Krebs (Kluane) holds predation the dominant driver and food a minor one, so 'plays a part as well' is a fair, not overstated, mention.

unit_notes: 10 questions: 8 ok, 1 error, 1 uncertain. Error (e97034add7, tick): the context lists Lyme disease as part of the deer's cost, but deer do not get Lyme disease (dead-end hosts); fix offered. Uncertain (efe145d475, lynx lag): key is right, but the stem says the HBC kept records of hare furs sold for close to a century; the classic hare series is fur records only for 1844-1904 and trapper questionnaires for 1905-1935 (Stenseth et al. 1997 PNAS); a safe rewording is offered. Optional wording notes (not errors): bile 'helps break down' rather than 'digests' fat (2cce2fac53); farmers did not know the soil gain was nitrogen (0a83478dc5); hare crashes are the work of several hunters, not lynx alone (b3da8b296b). Orchid-as-commensalism key judged safe: standard in Grokipedia and the epiphyte literature, and the context carries the 'hard to prove' caveat.
